newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Robotics -- from beat-up Mazda to personal jet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Robotics -- from beat-up Mazda to personal jet.

text.p: U.S. Robotics Corp, whose computer modems are on more desktops around the world than any other company's, said Wednesday it will give up its name and merge with 3Com Corp. in a stock merger valued at $6.6 billion.

The company, known for its Sportster and Courier modems and for being the first to market with 56-kilobit-per-second modem technology, became the darling of Wall Street in its relatively short stint, taking advantage of the Internet craze of the 1990s.
"They've become the bride, one of the most prized catches of networking," said Amar Senan, an analyst for investment bankers Volpe, Welty & Co.

"They've come from a humble analog company to one of the most formidable networking companies," Senan said. "They started with 300 (bits per second) modems" and just this week shipped their first 56 kilobit "x2" modems.

Casey Cowell, chairman and chief executive of U.S. Robotics, founded the company in 1976 with four college friends, working day and night in a windowless workroom above a military surplus store in Chicago.
The young company was cash-strapped, to say the least.

In a recent speech in Chicago, Cowell said in 1985 he and John McCartney, who serves as the company's president, drove to ask for financing from Mesirow Financial in a beat-up Mazda with no working doors and a passenger side window which did not roll down. To get in and out of the car you had to climb through the window on the driver's side, he said.

"One of the ways we've kind of measured how the company's done is essentially just, not even the comfort, just the reliability of the transportation we used, the mode of transportation," Cowell said in the speech after winning the "executive of the year" award from Crain's Chicago Business.

"As I was standing in the parking lot looking at the Mesirow Building and looking at this bright red (Mercedes) 450SL, in my car all I could see was McCartney's backside squeeze its way out of the window. I remember thinking, I'm really on the wrong end of this industry," he said.
"But we don't think that anymore," Cowell said. And today he takes his own personal jet.

The company's first modems were sold under the names of Apple Computer Inc and Commodore Computers. In 1987, the company began to focus on selling its own brand of products and posted revenues of $21 million. For fiscal 1996 which ended on September 30, U.S. Robotics reported revenues of $1.98 billion.
U.S. Robotics went public in October of 1991 at $13 a share. After stock splits, a $1,000 investment made in 1991 is worth about $30,000, he said.
